title: Packet Capture and Traffic Analysis with tcpdump

# Packet Capture and Traffic Analysis with `tcpdump`

When a service is misbehaving intermittently, connection diagnostics with `ss` tell you *that* traffic is failing — but they cannot tell you *what* is actually in the packets. That is where `tcpdump` comes in. It listens on a network interface and records every packet that flows through it, letting you see the raw conversation between two hosts in real time.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/tcpdump.svg)

`tcpdump` uses **Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF)** expressions to filter which packets it captures. BPF is a kernel-level filtering mechanism — expressions like `port 80`, `host 10.0.1.5`, or `tcp and not port 22` are compiled directly into kernel bytecode, so only matching packets ever leave the kernel. This makes `tcpdump` fast even on high-traffic interfaces.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Capture live packets on a network interface with `tcpdump`
- Use BPF filter expressions to isolate traffic by host, port, and protocol
- Write a capture to a `.pcap` file and read it back for offline analysis
- Interpret the basic fields in `tcpdump` output: timestamp, addresses, TCP flags, and payload length
- Use `tcpdump` to answer real diagnostic questions about what a service is actually sending

## The Scenario: Verifying a Service's Traffic

The `Poridhi.io` platform team has deployed a new internal service and needs to verify two things before it goes to production:

1. The service is actually receiving connections on the expected port
2. The traffic between components matches the expected protocol and payload structure

Your job is to run targeted packet captures and confirm the expected behaviour — and to spot anything that looks wrong. You will generate test traffic using tools already available on the VM and capture it with `tcpdump`.

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `lo` | Loopback interface — all localhost traffic flows here; safe to capture on without affecting the SSH session |
| `eth0` | Primary interface carrying your SSH session — observe only |
| Port `9090` | Simulated test service created with `netcat` |
| Port `8080` | HTTP test service created with Python |
| BPF filter | Kernel-level expression that controls which packets `tcpdump` captures |
| `.pcap` file | Binary file format for storing captured packets; readable by `tcpdump`, Wireshark, and other tools |

> **Note:** `tcpdump` only captures packets — it never modifies traffic. Running it on `eth0` is completely safe and will not affect your SSH session. For the practice captures in this lab we use `lo` (loopback), since all test traffic flows over localhost.

## Part 1: Understanding Packet Capture

When you run `sudo tcpdump -i lo`, the kernel copies each packet that arrives on the loopback interface into a ring buffer in memory. `tcpdump` reads from that buffer, applies the BPF filter you specified, and prints or saves only the matching packets.

### How a BPF Filter Works

A BPF filter is an expression written in `tcpdump`'s filter language. It is compiled into kernel bytecode and evaluated before any data leaves the kernel — so filtering is nearly free in terms of CPU overhead, even on busy interfaces:

| Expression | What it captures |
|-----------|-----------------|
| `port 80` | Any packet with source or destination port 80 |
| `host 10.0.1.5` | Any packet to or from that IP |
| `tcp` | TCP packets only |
| `udp port 53` | DNS queries and responses |
| `tcp and port 9090` | TCP traffic on port 9090 only |
| `not port 22` | Everything except SSH |
| `host 10.0.1.5 and port 80` | HTTP traffic to or from a specific host |

### Reading `tcpdump` Output

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/three-way-handshake.svg)

Each line in `tcpdump` output follows this format:

```
<timestamp> <protocol> <src-ip>.<src-port> > <dst-ip>.<dst-port>: Flags [<flags>], seq <n>, length <n>
```

For example:

```
12:34:56.789012 IP 127.0.0.1.45231 > 127.0.0.1.9090: Flags [S], seq 12345678, win 65535, length 0
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `12:34:56.789012` | Timestamp to microsecond precision |
| `IP` | Protocol family (IP, IP6, ARP, etc.) |
| `127.0.0.1.45231` | Source IP and port — port follows the last dot |
| `127.0.0.1.9090` | Destination IP and port |
| `Flags [S]` | TCP flags |
| `seq 12345678` | TCP sequence number |
| `length 0` | Payload length in bytes |

TCP flags to recognise:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `[S]` | SYN — connection initiation |
| `[S.]` | SYN-ACK — server accepting the connection |
| `[.]` | ACK — acknowledgement only, no data |
| `[P.]` | PSH-ACK — data is being pushed |
| `[F.]` | FIN-ACK — graceful connection close |
| `[R.]` | RST-ACK — abrupt connection reset |

A normal TCP connection always starts with `[S]` → `[S.]` → `[.]` (the three-way handshake), followed by `[P.]` packets carrying data, and ends with `[F.]` → `[.]` exchanges.

## Part 2: Exploring Your Network Traffic Baseline

Before generating any test traffic, take a short baseline capture of your VM. This gives you a reference point — you will see exactly how the output changes once you start the services in Part 3.

### Step 1: Capture Five Packets on the Primary Interface

At first, install `tcpdump` if not already installed:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y tcpdump
```

Then, capture 5 packets on the primary interface:

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 5 -n
```

The flags used here:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-i eth0` | Capture on the primary interface |
| `-c 5` | Stop automatically after 5 packets |
| `-n` | Do not resolve hostnames or port names — shows raw IPs and numbers |

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image.png)

This tells us the VM communicates with the outside world entirely through a WireGuard tunnel, which is why no raw SSH or HTTP traffic is visible — everything is encrypted inside the VPN. The kernel dropped zero packets, meaning the system handled the capture without any performance issues.

### Step 2: Check the Loopback Interface

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 3 -n
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-1.png)

The loopback interface carries traffic between processes on the same machine. You may see a few packets from system services. This is where all test traffic in Parts 4–6 will appear once you start the services in Part 3.

> **Note:** Do not modify anything in this part. This is observation only.

## Part 3: Setting Up the Lab Environment

We will start two services to generate capturable traffic.

### Step 1: Install Required Tools

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y netcat-openbsd
```

`netcat-openbsd` gives us `nc` for creating TCP listeners and connections. `tcpdump` is already installed on the Poridhi lab VM.

### Step 2: Start a Listener on Port 9090

Open a **second terminal** and start a netcat listener — this is our simulated service:

```bash
# Terminal 2 — keep this running
nc -lk 9090
```

The `-l` flag puts `nc` into listen mode. `-k` keeps it alive after each client disconnects so it continues accepting new connections.

### Step 3: Start an HTTP Server on Port 8080

Open a **third terminal** and start Python's built-in HTTP server:

```bash
# Terminal 3 — keep this running
python3 -m http.server 8080
```

We now have two services listening on localhost. All their traffic flows over the loopback interface — ready to be captured.

## Part 4: Capturing Traffic with `tcpdump`

### Step 1: Capture All Traffic on the Loopback Interface

Back in **Terminal 1**, start a live capture:

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -n
```

While the capture is running, open a fourth terminal and connect to the netcat listener:

```bash
echo "hello from tcpdump" | nc localhost 9090
```

You will see the full lifecycle of the connection: the three-way handshake (`[S]` → `[S.]` → `[.]`), the data packet (`[P.]` with a non-zero length), and the teardown (`[F.]` → `[.]`). This is the complete picture of a short-lived TCP connection.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-2.png)

Press `Ctrl+C` to stop. `tcpdump` prints a summary: packets received by the filter, dropped by the kernel (buffer overflow on busy systems), and dropped by the interface driver.

We can also see the message in the netcat listener on the second terminal.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-3.png)

### Step 2: Limit the Capture Count

Running indefinitely is useful interactively but not in scripts. The `-c` flag stops the capture automatically:

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 10 -n
```

Generate traffic in another terminal while this runs:

```bash
echo "test" | nc localhost 9090
```

`tcpdump` exits as soon as 10 packets are captured — no manual `Ctrl+C` needed. This is the standard form for automated captures in monitoring scripts.

### Step 3: Increase Verbosity

By default, `tcpdump` shows one line per packet. The `-v` flag adds extra IP-layer fields (TTL, total length, IP ID):

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 5 -n -v
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-4.png)

`-vv` adds full protocol decoding and `-vvv` is maximum verbosity. For most diagnostic work, `-v` is the right level — enough detail without being overwhelming.

### Step 4: Show Packet Contents in ASCII

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/response%20flow.svg)

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 10 -n -A port 8080
```

While this capture runs, generate an HTTP request:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080 > /dev/null
```

`-A` prints the packet payload as ASCII after each packet header. For HTTP traffic, you will see the `GET / HTTP/1.1` request line and `HTTP/1.0 200 OK` response headers — confirming exactly what the application is sending, not just that it is sending something.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-5.png)

**Why it matters**: Being able to see raw traffic in real time is the difference between guessing what an application is doing and knowing. `tcpdump` shows you the actual bytes on the wire — including headers that application-layer logs never expose.

## Part 5: Filtering Traffic

### Step 1: Filter by Port

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 10 -n port 9090
```

Generate traffic on port 9090 while this runs:

```bash
echo "filtered by port" | nc localhost 9090
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-6.png)

Only packets with source or destination port `9090` appear. The HTTP server traffic on port 8080 is completely excluded — even if it is generating packets at the same time.

### Step 2: Filter by Host

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 10 -n host 8.8.8.8
```

Generate a DNS request while this runs:

```bash
sudo ping -c 2 8.8.8.8
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-7.png)

Only packets to or from `8.8.8.8` are shown. On a production server, replacing `8.8.8.8` with a database IP or an external API address lets you isolate exactly the traffic between two specific hosts from among thousands of concurrent flows.

### Step 3: Filter by Protocol

```bash
# Only TCP
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 10 -n tcp

# Only ICMP (ping packets)
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 5 -n icmp
```

For the ICMP capture, open another terminal and run `ping -c 3 8.8.8.8` while the capture is running:

You will see the ICMP echo requests (`ICMP echo request`) and replies (`ICMP echo reply`) as separate packets (Same as Step 2 before this). Protocol filtering is the fastest way to scope a capture when you know the protocol involved but not the specific port.

### Step 4: Combine Filters with `and`, `or`, `not`

BPF expressions compose with boolean operators. Quoting the expression avoids shell interpretation issues:

```bash
# TCP traffic on port 9090 only
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 10 -n "tcp and port 9090"

# Port 8080 or port 9090
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 10 -n "port 8080 or port 9090"

# Everything on eth0 except SSH
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 10 -n "not port 22"
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-8.png)

The `not port 22` filter is essential when capturing on `eth0`. Without it, your own SSH session floods the output with packets, making it impossible to see the traffic you are actually investigating.

**Why it matters**: On a production server with thousands of packets per second, an unfiltered `tcpdump` capture is unusable. BPF filters are the difference between a targeted diagnostic tool and an unusable firehose. Precise filter expressions are one of the highest-leverage skills in network troubleshooting.

## Part 6: Reading and Writing `.pcap` Files

Capturing to a file lets you investigate traffic offline, share captures with a colleague, or load them into Wireshark for graphical analysis.

### Step 1: Write a Capture to File

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 20 -n -w /tmp/lab17.pcap
```

While the capture is running, generate traffic on both services from another terminal:

```bash
echo "saved payload" | nc localhost 9090
curl -s http://localhost:8080 > /dev/null
```

When the 20-packet limit is reached, `tcpdump` stops. The file `/tmp/lab17.pcap` now contains all captured packets in standard pcap format.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-9.png)

### Step 2: Read a Capture File

```bash
tcpdump -r /tmp/lab17.pcap -n
```

Reading a `.pcap` file does not require `sudo` and does not need an active interface — the data is on disk. The output looks identical to a live capture, including the original timestamps from when the packets were captured.

### Step 3: Apply Filters When Reading

BPF filters work exactly the same way when reading from a file as they do in live captures:

```bash
# Show only port 9090 traffic
tcpdump -r /tmp/lab17.pcap -n port 9090

# Show only port 8080 traffic
tcpdump -r /tmp/lab17.pcap -n port 8080

# Show only SYN packets (the start of each connection)
tcpdump -r /tmp/lab17.pcap -n "tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0"
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-10.png)

The last filter uses a byte-offset expression: `tcp[tcpflags]` reads the TCP flags byte directly from the packet header, and `& tcp-syn != 0` checks whether the SYN bit is set. This isolates only the first packet of each connection — useful for counting how many distinct connections were initiated in a capture file.

**Why it matters**: Saving captures to `.pcap` is standard practice in network diagnostics. You capture once, then apply different filters repeatedly to examine the same data from different angles — without having to reproduce the traffic.

## Part 7: Answering the Investigation Questions

Let's use what we have learned to answer the platform team's original questions.

### Q1: Is the service actually receiving connections on port 9090?

```bash
# Start the capture
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 6 -n "tcp and port 9090"

# Generate a connection
echo "probe" | nc localhost 9090
```

A healthy connection shows the full handshake: `[S]` → `[S.]` → `[.]`, followed by a `[P.]` packet with a non-zero length (the data), and a `[F.]` teardown. If you see `[S]` followed immediately by `[R]` (reset), the port is not actually listening — the kernel rejected the connection.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/b6e8c7eced2c458d6754a167fb73ee927f0b6b83/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2017/images/image-11.png)

### Q2: What does the HTTP traffic on port 8080 look like at the packet level?

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -c 10 -n -A "tcp and port 8080"
curl -s http://localhost:8080 > /dev/null
```

The `-A` flag reveals the full HTTP conversation: the `GET / HTTP/1.1` request with `Host:` and `User-Agent:` headers, and the `HTTP/1.0 200 OK` response. This confirms what the application is actually sending — not just that it is sending something.

### Q3: Is there any unexpected traffic leaving the server?

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 20 -n "not port 22"
```

Filtering out SSH leaves only non-SSH traffic on the primary interface. On a correctly configured server, you should see only expected traffic — WireGuard UDP packets, ICMP, and perhaps DNS. Any unexpected destination IP or an unknown high-numbered port warrants immediate investigation.

## Conclusion

In this lab, we used `tcpdump` to move from "something is wrong with this connection" to "here is exactly what is happening at the packet level":

- `tcpdump -i <iface>` starts a live, read-only capture on any interface without affecting the traffic it observes
- BPF filter expressions (`port`, `host`, `tcp`, `not`, `and`, `or`) isolate exactly the traffic you need from a potentially noisy interface
- `-A` reveals the ASCII payload — the difference between confirming a connection exists and seeing what it is actually sending

`tcpdump` sits at the lowest level of network diagnostics — below application logs, below `ss`, below everything except the raw interface itself. When all other tools give inconclusive answers, `tcpdump` shows you the truth of what is on the wire.
